reason: The sources support a highly engaging narrative with at least 14 claims verified across multiple independent sites.
story: Before humans reached the Moon, a terrifying theory threatened to ground the entire Apollo program. Cornell astronomer Thomas Gold warned that the lunar surface was covered in a deep, bottomless layer of fine dust that would swallow spacecraft like quicksand. To test this, NASA launched the Surveyor program. In 1966, Surveyor 1 proved the ground was firm, basaltic rock. Yet, the soil held an electrifying secret: solar radiation and solar wind charge the dust, forcing it to levitate up to kilometers high. This electrostatic fountain creates a eerie twilight glow, witnessed by robotic cameras and Apollo crews alike. In 1969, Apollo 12 demonstrated the precision needed to navigate this harsh environment by landing within walking distance of the robotic Surveyor 3 probe. The deep-dust quicksand myth was thoroughly busted, but the real Moon proved to be an active, hovering electrostatic dust storm.
angle: Scientists genuinely feared the Moon was covered in bottomless 'Gold dust' quicksand that would swallow spacecraft, but the real soil turned out to be an electrifying, levitating dust fountain.

claims.claim: Cornell astronomer Thomas Gold theorized that the Moon was covered in a deep layer of fine dust that would swallow landers.
The Soviet Union's Luna 9 achieved the world's first robotic soft landing on the Moon in February 1966.
Surveyor 1 was the first American spacecraft to make a controlled soft landing on the Moon in June 1966.
Surveyor 5 carried an instrument that performed the first on-site chemical analysis of lunar soil.
Surveyor 5's chemical analysis revealed the Moon's soil is basaltic in composition, resembling Earth's volcanic rock.
Hal Clement's 1956 sci-fi story 'Dust Rag' anticipated the electrostatic levitation of lunar dust.
Surveyor cameras photographed a twilight glow over the lunar horizon after sunset.
Apollo 17 astronauts witnessed and sketched twilight rays or streamers before lunar sunrise or sunset.
On the Moon's daylit side, solar UV and X-ray radiation knock electrons out of soil atoms, building up positive charges.
On the night side, electrons from the solar wind charge the dust negatively.
The tiny, charged dust particles repel each other and are lofted from meters to kilometers high.
Apollo 12 landed within walking distance of the robotic probe Surveyor 3 in November 1969.
Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked to Surveyor 3 and retrieved parts of it to bring back to Earth.
Surveyor 6 performed the first liftoff from another celestial body by hopping off the surface.

disputed: The exact landing distance between Apollo 12 and Surveyor 3 is disputed (160 meters in S4 vs 180 meters in S5). The script should reconcile this by saying 'about 160 to 180 meters'.

Whether Neil Armstrong shut down the Lunar Module engine before touchdown. S2 notes Armstrong fired the engine until touchdown, while other missions experienced noticeable bumps by shutting it down early. The script should focus on the dust effects rather than this engineering debate.
